edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SPORT + SCIENCE & TECHNOLOGY
edition.deck: War, justice and political pressure feature in a day of consequential developments, alongside scrutiny of health services and stories from Denmark.
edition.editorialNote: Stories are grouped by underlying event and assigned to one canonical section. Danish-language source reporting has been translated into English; allegations and unresolved questions remain attributed.

content.headline: Pentagon says Nidal Hasan’s execution will be livestreamed
content.shortHeadline: US plans livestream of Fort Hood shooter’s execution
content.standfirst: The Pentagon says Nidal Hasan is due to be executed by firing squad at Fort Hood on 3 December. Legal experts cited in the reporting warn that court proceedings could delay or challenge the plan.

image.caption: Nidal Malik Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009.

sources.originalTitle: Fort Hood attacker's execution by firing squad will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
Pentagon says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
Pentagon: Henrettelse af mand bag massedrab på militærbase skal livestreames
Hegseth vil livestreame henrettelse

segments.body: The Pentagon says it plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the former US Army psychiatrist sentenced to death for killing 13 soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth says a firing squad will carry out the sentence at the Texas base on 3 December.

segments.title: Legal questions remain
segments.body: The BBC reports that Hasan’s appellate process is not over and that he may seek federal review, which could stay the execution. The Guardian says he exhausted his appeals last year. The Pentagon has named a date, but the supplied reporting does not resolve how the legal process affects it.

perspectives.body: The Guardian adds that there is no record of Barack Obama using the phrase “workplace violence” for the 2009 attack, despite Hegseth’s claim, and details the way that classification affected victims’ eligibility for combat-related benefits.

segments.title: An unprecedented public spectacle
segments.body: The BBC describes livestreaming a US execution as unprecedented in the modern era. Legal experts raise questions about the legality and practicalities of broadcasting it; the BBC also reports that it remains unclear where the stream would be available and whether platforms would permit it.

content.headline: Russian strike on buses kills at least 30 in Kramatorsk, officials say
content.shortHeadline: At least 30 killed in strike on buses in Kramatorsk
content.standfirst: Ukrainian officials say two civilian buses were hit in the eastern city, with another 18 people wounded. The attack comes amid a sharp rise in civilian casualties and repeated strikes across Ukraine.

image.caption: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called for more international support after the attack.

sources.originalTitle: Russian strike on buses kills at least 30, say officials, as deadly attacks on Ukraine surge

segments.body: At least 30 people were killed and 18 wounded in a Russian glide-bomb attack on two civilian buses in Kramatorsk, Ukrainian officials say. Three more people were killed in nearby Bilenke. Russia had not commented on the attack in the supplied report.

segments.title: A wider toll
segments.body: The attack is part of a worsening pattern, the BBC reports. The UN says more civilians had been killed in Ukraine by August this year than in all of 2025. A separate strike on an apartment block in Pryluky killed 22 people, including five children, while attacks have also disrupted Kyiv’s transport, power and water supplies.

Donetsk regional head Vadym Filashkin accused Russia of targeting buses carrying passengers to kill civilians. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the strike would not go unanswered and called on Ukraine’s partners to provide more defence support. Local authorities ordered public transport to stop in the area and urged residents to move to safer parts of the country.

content.headline: ICE agent shoots man in New York as mayor calls for facts
content.shortHeadline: ICE agent shoots man in New York; child reportedly unharmed
content.standfirst: The Department of Homeland Security says an officer fired during an operation in the Bronx and that the man is alive. New York’s mayor says a five-year-old was in the car; the governor has asked for body-camera footage to be released.

sources.originalTitle: ICE agent shoots man in New York City
Borgmester: ICE-agenter skød mand i New York, mens barn befandt sig i bilen

segments.body: An ICE agent shot a man in the Bronx on Thursday during what the Department of Homeland Security described as a targeted operation to arrest a person it called a “criminal illegal alien”. The man was taken to hospital and was alive, the department said.

segments.title: Accounts and calls for evidence
segments.body: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said early reports indicated that agents surrounded the man and a five-year-old child in his car before firing multiple rounds. He said the child appeared physically unharmed. Governor Kathy Hochul said she asked President Donald Trump for any body-camera footage to be made public; the report does not say whether it will be released.

DHS said the unnamed man was from the Dominican Republic and listed prior convictions and arrests, as well as an alleged association with the Trinitarios gang. Mamdani said he would ask Trump to end ICE enforcement actions in New York. The supplied reporting does not establish the circumstances of the shooting independently.

content.headline: BBC finds US and Lebanon sheltering wanted Syrian general
content.shortHeadline: Wanted Syrian general reportedly sheltered in Lebanon
content.standfirst: A BBC and NPR investigation says Bassam al-Hassan has been protected and funded in Lebanon under an arrangement tied to information about abducted US journalist Austin Tice. The FBI declined to comment on the findings.

image.caption: Bassam al-Hassan is wanted over alleged crimes committed under Syria’s Assad regime.

sources.originalTitle: US and Lebanon protecting wanted Syrian general, BBC finds

segments.body: A BBC and NPR investigation says Bassam al-Hassan, a former Syrian general wanted over alleged crimes against humanity, has been allowed to remain in Lebanon under an arrangement involving US and Lebanese authorities. The reporting says he is providing information, including about the 2012 abduction of US journalist Austin Tice.

segments.title: Questions over the arrangement
segments.body: The BBC says sources described Hassan receiving money through an intermediary and being offered residency, protection and help with living costs. People connected to the Tice investigation told the broadcasters they had seen little evidence that his information had significantly advanced the case. The FBI declined to comment on the findings.

Officials from two branches of Syria’s new government told the BBC they want Hassan returned to face trial. The Tice family’s spokesperson said that, if the findings are true, using public money to support someone associated with chemical weapons and the alleged execution of Tice would be offensive. Hassan has said Tice was executed on Bashar al-Assad’s orders, but sources have questioned parts of his account; a search at a location he identified found no remains, though the BBC says there are questions about how thoroughly it was searched.

content.headline: French government promises teachers as student protests continue
content.shortHeadline: France promises substitute teachers amid protests
content.standfirst: France says it will deploy 3,000 substitute teachers to schools facing acute shortages, but student organisers say the response falls short. Protests have spread across the country, with clashes and injuries reported.

image.caption: Students gather at the Place de la Bastille during protests in Paris.

sources.originalTitle: French ministers scramble to appease students after 10 days of protests
France's school protests: What lies behind the anger
Unges protester inspirerer: 'Lad os gøre som i Frankrig'
En afreven hånd og en knust kæbe får velkendt kritik af fransk politi til at blusse op

segments.body: France’s education minister, Édouard Geffray, said 3,000 substitute teachers would be sent to about 100 high schools with acute shortages, with “several hundred” more teachers to be recruited. The announcement came as students continued protests over staffing, dilapidated buildings and long school days.

segments.title: Protesters say measures are not enough
segments.body: Student representatives said they had received no concrete response to their demands and would continue demonstrations. The Guardian reported more than 71,000 people took to the streets on Thursday, while the education ministry said 224 schools were closed in the morning and 157 by lunchtime. A poll cited in the reporting found 72% considered the demands legitimate, while 55% thought the protests should stop.

segments.title: Clashes and concern over policing
segments.body: Demonstrations have included clashes with police and injuries among students, school staff and officers. The government suspended the use of stun grenades after a teenager lost a hand, while the BBC reports that France’s wider political gridlock and pressure to reduce public borrowing limit the government’s room to fund demands. Separate Danish coverage describes protests and concerns about police tactics; these accounts add context but do not establish a single cause or view across the movement.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s analysis puts the protests in the context of France’s tradition of street mobilisation, while noting that grievances alone do not explain the movement’s scale. It says the financially constrained government may have little room to make concessions.

content.headline: German former spy chief held as prosecutors investigate alleged espionage
content.shortHeadline: Former German spy chief investigated over secret files
content.standfirst: August Hanning is accused of obtaining thousands of classified documents and using them in analysis for a foreign intelligence service. Reporting points to possible Azerbaijani links, but investigators have not named the suspected recipient.

image.caption: August Hanning headed Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service from 1998 to 2005.

sources.originalTitle: The hidden clues that link Russia to German ‘super-spy’ scandal
German spy suspect mixed with UK spooks… without ever being trusted
The UK security risks after German spy chief arrested, according to experts

segments.body: German prosecutors allege that August Hanning, who led Germany’s foreign intelligence service from 1998 to 2005, arranged to receive around 2,000 sensitive documents from a former aide who remained in the agency. Hanning was arrested on suspicion of espionage and treason; his lawyer says he is being unjustly prosecuted and denies passing information to Germany’s detriment or receiving payment.

segments.title: Possible foreign links remain unconfirmed
segments.body: German media have reported that prosecutors are examining whether an analysis allegedly written by Hanning was intended for Azerbaijan’s intelligence service. Investigators have not established whether it reached its intended recipient, and Russia is not currently part of the inquiry, according to the supplied reports. The i Paper reports that the documents included material on Russia’s military and Iran’s nuclear programme.

perspectives.body: Former British intelligence chiefs quoted by the i Paper say information-sharing with Germany was more controlled than with some allies because of longstanding concerns about possible leaks. They also say shared intelligence is often sanitised to reduce risks.

segments.title: Potential implications for allies
segments.body: The i Paper reports that British services are reviewing intelligence shared during any period considered vulnerable. Experts differ on the scale of the danger: one warns of possible disinformation, while another stresses that identities of officers and agents are protected. The investigation has not established that UK intelligence was compromised.

content.headline: Venezuelan former judge says she was threatened into barring Machado
content.shortHeadline: Venezuelan judge says threats forced Machado ban
content.standfirst: Barbara César Siero says relatives were detained in 2023 to pressure her into signing documents that included a ban on opposition leader María Corina Machado standing for election. The claim comes from an interview with AFP.

sources.originalTitle: Venezuelansk dommer: Jeg blev truet til at udelukke Nobelprismodtager

segments.body: Former Venezuelan Supreme Court judge Barbara César Siero says she signed the 2023 decision barring opposition leader María Corina Machado from standing for election after two of her brothers and her sister-in-law were detained. Siero says the three relatives, who work in the military, were held to pressure her.

Siero told AFP she was given eight documents to sign after the arrests. “Maybe if I sign, they’ll release them,” she recalled thinking. She says she signed, but the relatives remained in custody. The supplied report does not include a response from the former government to her allegation.

content.headline: Court rules Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor search warrants unlawful
content.shortHeadline: Andrew search warrants ruled unlawful; investigation continues
content.standfirst: Thames Valley Police accepted that the warrants used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s homes were issued under the wrong legal provision. Police still hold seized material while a further hearing considers whether they can retain it.

image.caption: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor remains under investigation over alleged misconduct in public office.

sources.originalTitle: Warrants used to search Andrew's homes were unlawful, court says
Search warrants used in Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor raids were unlawful, court rules
Andrew wins legal claim against police over search of his homes

segments.body: The High Court has been told that Thames Valley Police accepted search warrants used at Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s homes were unlawful because the wrong provision of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act was used. The warrants were quashed, but the court said the decision does not end the criminal investigation.

segments.title: Evidence still in police hands
segments.body: Police continue to hold documents and electronic devices seized during searches of his homes. Mountbatten-Windsor opposes their application to retain the material under alternative powers; a further hearing is expected in 2027. A judge will have to decide whether it can be kept and used as evidence.

perspectives.body: The Guardian explains that the incorrect warrant provision carries safeguards for legally privileged and other confidential material. A former CPS specialist says the police may ultimately be allowed to keep some or all of the seized material, but that decision has not yet been made.

segments.body: Mountbatten-Windsor was arrested in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office following allegations that he shared confidential information with Jeffrey Epstein while serving as a UK trade envoy. He denies wrongdoing. Thames Valley Police says the warrant ruling is not a judgment on its ongoing investigation.

content.headline: NHS review urges needs-led mental health, ADHD and autism support
content.shortHeadline: NHS review calls for help without waiting for diagnosis
content.standfirst: A government-commissioned review says rising mental distress is real and services risk failing under mounting demand. It recommends support based on need rather than diagnosis, while warning about assessment quality and possible overdiagnosis.

image.caption: The review says mental distress has risen across age groups in England, especially among under-18s.

sources.originalTitle: NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds
No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are real
NHS England mental health services review: what has it found and what does it recommend?

segments.body: A review of mental health, ADHD and autism services in England says demand has risen sharply and the NHS risks “system failures” without major change. More than 560,000 people were waiting for an ADHD assessment and 254,000 for an autism assessment at the end of last year, with most waiting at least three months.

segments.title: Support should not depend on a label
segments.body: The review led by Prof Peter Fonagy recommends bringing mental health and neurodevelopmental services together and providing help according to people’s needs, rather than making diagnosis the only route to support. It says young people’s distress is real and cannot be explained by greater awareness alone; the report also points to financial insecurity, housing costs and lack of hope among pressures on young people.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis highlights the review’s rejection of the “snowflake generation” caricature and its argument that waiting lists and diagnosis-gated support create unfairness, particularly for people unable to afford private assessment.

segments.title: Quality and overdiagnosis concerns
segments.body: The review does not find overdiagnosis occurring at scale, but says the balance of risks may be changing as diagnoses rise. It raises concerns about the consistency of private assessments and calls for clinics to be regulated and direct-to-public advertising banned. Health Secretary Yvette Cooper backs regulation but has not committed to the advertising ban.

content.headline: Labour wins Holborn and St Pancras byelection against Greens
content.shortHeadline: Labour holds Starmer’s former seat in byelection
content.standfirst: Sagal Abdi-Wali beat Green leader Zack Polanski in the north London contest, which had the lowest byelection turnout in England during this parliament. The result offers Labour relief in a high-profile contest on the left.

image.caption: Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali won the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.

sources.originalTitle: Labour fends off Green party to win Holborn and St Pancras byelection

segments.body: Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali won the Holborn and St Pancras byelection with 12,292 votes, ahead of Green leader Zack Polanski on 8,928. The seat was vacated by Keir Starmer in September. Turnout was 38.7%, down 15.4 percentage points from the 2024 general election.

segments.title: A test for the Greens
segments.body: The Greens conceded defeat, saying their campaign in a Labour stronghold showed how far the party had come. The result followed internal controversy over a party motion on Zionism; Polanski missed the debate and did not vote. Former Green leader Caroline Lucas said he should show leadership on the issue.

Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee from Somalia and leader of Camden Council, becomes Labour’s new MP. The Guardian reports that Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf was accused by Labour of racism after comments about her candidacy; the report does not provide his response to that accusation.

content.headline: Royal Navy sailor charged with preparing to pass secrets to foreign power
content.shortHeadline: Navy intelligence sailor charged over alleged spying
content.standfirst: Teddy Young, 24, is accused of retaining sensitive defence material and preparing to pass it to an unnamed foreign power. He was first arrested in 2025 and has been remanded in custody; the allegations have not been tested in court.

image.caption: Teddy Young appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court after being charged.

sources.originalTitle: Royal Navy sailor charged with spying ‘was working for Russia’

segments.body: Royal Navy sailor Teddy Young has been charged under the National Security Act with offences relating to sensitive defence and intelligence material. Prosecutors allege he retained protected information and engaged in activity consistent with preparing to pass it to an unnamed foreign power. He has been remanded in custody.

segments.title: Investigation and safeguards
segments.body: Young was first arrested in May 2025 and had his security clearance suspended, according to the i Paper. The alleged conduct spans November 2024 to May 2025. Counter Terrorism Policing says it worked with the Ministry of Defence to mitigate risks; the Royal Navy says it would be inappropriate to comment while proceedings are ongoing.

The i Paper quotes experts who say a junior rank does not necessarily rule out access to sensitive material. They discuss possible recruitment, ideological motives or financial temptation, but no motive has been established and police say the case is not connected to the RAF Fairford inquiry.

content.headline: Asos breach exposed customer addresses, birth dates and searches, BBC finds
content.shortHeadline: Asos hackers accessed detailed customer profiles
content.standfirst: Asos says criminals accessed customer profiles that may include names, addresses, dates of birth and searches, but not passwords or bank details. The retailer has not said how many people were affected.

sources.originalTitle: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds

segments.body: Asos has told customers that hackers accessed detailed personal profiles, including names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, customer numbers, dates of birth and searches made on the site. The retailer says bank details and passwords were not accessed, but has not disclosed the scale of the breach.

segments.title: Risk of follow-up scams
segments.body: A customer whose data was shared with the BBC said it was unsettling to know criminals had personal details and shopping searches. Security experts warn the information could be used to make phishing messages or calls seem convincing. Asos advises customers to be wary of unsolicited contact and says it will never ask for passwords or payment details that way.

The BBC says the hackers contacted it with a sample of the data and that it delayed publication to allow Asos to contact customers. The company says an employee account was accessed after login credentials were obtained through impersonation. Snowflake says its platform was not breached; the hackers claim they used a service built on it, a claim not established by the supplied reporting.

content.headline: Dossier at murder suspect’s home named more than 100 public figures
content.shortHeadline: Police contacted politicians named in suspect’s dossier
content.standfirst: A dossier found at the home of a man charged with Ann Widdecombe’s murder reportedly included senior politicians and other public figures. The discovery raises questions about when those named were warned and whether extra security was needed.

image.caption: Joshua Kerry appeared at Westminster Magistrates’ Court.

sources.originalTitle: Badenoch on list found in home of Widdecombe suspect

segments.body: A dossier found at the home of Joshua Kerry, who is charged with murdering former Tory minister Ann Widdecombe, reportedly named more than 100 prominent people, including Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch and members of her shadow cabinet. Police have contacted people named in the material in recent days, the i Paper reports.

segments.title: Questions about warnings
segments.body: The report says the material was found during searches after Kerry’s arrest in July and raises questions about whether police warned those named promptly. It says even the Speaker of the House of Commons may not have been given a list of affected MPs. The Met and Home Office had not responded to the paper’s earlier questions about the list.

Kerry is also charged with preparing acts of terrorism, including against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage. Prosecutors have alleged online reconnaissance and an attempted entry to Farage’s home; the charges have not been proven. Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the developments raise serious questions about security for people in public life.

content.headline: Survey finds Ofsted inspections still harm school staff wellbeing
content.shortHeadline: Most surveyed school leaders say Ofsted harms staff wellbeing
content.standfirst: An independent survey commissioned by Ofsted found 88% of responding school leaders said inspections negatively affected staff mental health. The findings are limited because fewer than one in four schools agreed to take part.

image.caption: School leaders say Ofsted inspections continue to put pressure on staff wellbeing.

sources.originalTitle: New Ofsted inspection regime damaging teachers, survey says

segments.body: An independent survey commissioned by Ofsted found that 88% of school leaders who responded said inspections under the revised system had negatively affected staff mental wellbeing; 29% said the impact was substantial. Fewer than one in four schools agreed to take part, and the researchers noted that limitation.

segments.title: Disagreement over the results
segments.body: Ofsted chief inspector Martyn Oliver said the findings showed the regulator was on the right track, pointing to respondents who said inspections were respectful and helped identify strengths. School leaders’ representatives rejected that assessment, saying the results showed persistent pressure and calling for the full data to be published.

The survey follows the 2023 coroner’s finding that an Ofsted inspection contributed to the deterioration in headteacher Ruth Perry’s mental health and death. Education Secretary Lucy Powell has reportedly called for the new inspection format to be reconsidered.

content.headline: Forever chemical found in English rivers and groundwater, tests show
content.shortHeadline: TFA found at nearly every English water site tested
content.standfirst: Environment Agency tests detected trifluoroacetic acid at all 50 surface-water sites and 43 of 49 groundwater sites. Scientists say health risks and future levels are still being studied; there is no UK limit for TFA in water.

image.caption: The highest TFA concentration in surface water was found in the River Ancholme in Lincolnshire.

sources.originalTitle: Forever chemical linked to fertility issues found in rivers in England

segments.body: Environment Agency tests from 2024 found trifluoroacetic acid, or TFA, at all 50 surface-water sites tested in England and 43 of 49 groundwater sites. The highest surface-water reading was in the River Ancholme in Lincolnshire, while the highest groundwater reading was near Finchingfield in Essex.

segments.title: What is known—and not known
segments.body: TFA is a persistent chemical in the PFAS family. The European Chemicals Agency has recommended classifying it as a presumed reproductive toxicant based on animal studies, not human evidence. One expert said the levels detected were not necessarily high enough to trigger health problems now, but expressed concern that they appear to be rising.

There is currently no UK limit for TFA in water. Scientists say it can come from the breakdown of other PFAS, pesticides and fluorinated gases, and can reach water through runoff and the atmosphere. The Drinking Water Inspectorate is studying the risks; results are expected early next year. The supplied reporting says it is not clear whether treatment removes TFA.

content.headline: Danish government plan would cut support for more students
content.shortHeadline: More students face cuts under Danish grant proposal
content.standfirst: A draft budget would reduce grants for students living with parents whose income is as low as about 420,000 kroner a year, expanding a proposal first described as affecting those with higher-earning parents. The government’s budget is due to be presented formally.

sources.originalTitle: Endnu flere unge end ventet står til at få skåret i SU’en, viser finanslovsudspil

segments.body: A Danish government budget proposal would reduce education grants for more students living with their parents than first announced. The draft would phase down support for students whose parents earn about 420,000 to 710,000 kroner a year, and remove it for some above that range, according to DR.

segments.title: Other budget measures
segments.body: The proposal also includes 900 million kroner a year for primary schools, more money for defence, and funding for cheaper public transport and dental care, among other items. It would make electric cars above a specified price more expensive by ending an exemption from registration tax, and change graduate unemployment-benefit rules.

Alternativeet finance spokesperson Anna Bjerre criticised the grant cuts, saying students should not lose support because of their parents’ income. The budget was due to be presented officially on Friday morning; the supplied report describes the proposal, not its final passage.

content.headline: Greenland debates tougher alcohol rules as minister urges caution
content.shortHeadline: Greenland weighs tougher alcohol rules after calls for action
content.standfirst: Greenland’s health council recommends measures including a higher purchase age and limits on sales, while the health minister says parties must first agree on policy. Treatment providers say families, particularly children, are already bearing the effects.

image.caption: Greenland’s health minister says parties need to agree on an alcohol policy.

sources.originalTitle: Grønlands sundhedsminister tøver med alkohol-stramninger
Malene brød den onde cirkel: I Grønland har vi ikke været gode nok til at tale om alkohol

segments.body: Greenland’s health council says alcohol-related problems are serious enough to require stronger measures. Its recommendations include raising the minimum purchase age from 18 to 21, creating a sales monopoly and limiting weekend sales. Health Minister Anna Wangenheim says political talks should begin soon, but has not committed to specific changes.

segments.title: Disagreement over the response
segments.body: A Nuuk addiction-treatment provider says the government should act quickly, warning that alcohol problems affect families and children. Wangenheim says she is proceeding carefully because parties have different views and the social setting matters: she notes that harmful drinking also takes place in private homes, not only bars.

segments.title: One woman’s recovery
segments.body: DR’s separate report follows Malene Petersen, who says she stopped drinking in 2011 after years of depression and alcohol use. She hopes people will speak more openly about difficulties. Greenland’s health council says more than 40% of the population may have an alcohol problem, despite overall consumption having fallen.

content.headline: Energinet changes power-line route after public objections
content.shortHeadline: Revised power-line route spares one couple’s home
content.standfirst: Energinet has changed parts of its planned route for 44-metre transmission pylons after receiving about 250 public proposals. The revisions spare one couple’s property, but the company says other residents will still lose their homes.

image.caption: Mette and Brian Breitenstein are relieved the revised route will spare their home.

sources.originalTitle: Endelig plan for omstridte elmaster klar - Mette og Brian blev reddet på målstregen

segments.body: State-owned grid operator Energinet has published a revised route for high-voltage lines carrying electricity from eastern Lolland through South Zealand towards Herfølge. Three major changes move sections of the route, including one to the western side of the South Motorway near Sonnerup and Algestrup.

segments.title: Public input reshaped the plan
segments.body: Energinet says it reviewed about 250 proposals received after a public meeting and made both smaller adjustments and three substantial route changes. Mette and Brian Breitenstein, whose home had been in the way of the earlier plan, say they feel heard and relieved that the revised route no longer requires them to give up their property.

The dispute has also concerned why some sections of the connection will be buried while others will use overhead pylons. Energinet says burying more of the route would be too costly and affect electricity quality. The company acknowledges that the final plan will still require some residents to lose their homes.

content.headline: Why the shift from rural Denmark to cities strains local budgets
content.shortHeadline: Rural councils lose working-age residents to city regions
content.standfirst: Experts say the movement of working-age residents towards larger cities is widening the financial gap between Danish municipalities. Some families are moving to rural areas, but that remains a smaller countertrend.

image.caption: DR’s reporting contrasts housing demand in Høje-Taastrup with the difficulties facing Lemvig.

sources.originalTitle: Er der håb? Ja, siger eksperter: 'Jeg ville først for alvor være bekymret, hvis det kun var i de store byer, man trivedes'
Jan Isaksen knipser med fingrene. Det går bare stærkt! Men det er kun halvdelen af historien: For det kommer med en pris, kan hans kollega bevidne
Hvor vil du helst bo? Svaret på det spørgsmål er vigtigere, end du tror - og ikke kun for dig selv

segments.body: The share of working-age residents has fallen in many rural municipalities and risen in places near major cities, putting pressure on local tax bases, according to reporting by DR. Lemvig has seen one of the steepest declines outside island municipalities, while Høje-Taastrup has recorded strong growth.

segments.title: A self-reinforcing cycle
segments.body: Researchers say the imbalance is linked to people moving for work and education, an ageing population and low birth rates. Fewer working-age residents can mean less local revenue and fewer families to sustain schools and services, while a lack of jobs may make it harder for people who studied elsewhere to return.

perspectives.body: DR also follows a family that moved from Valby to Møn for space, nature and proximity to grandparents. Experts describe such moves as a countertrend and argue that life outside the largest cities can remain attractive.

segments.body: The scale differs between municipalities: DR reports that the working-age population in Lemvig fell by 8.5% over six years, while it grew by 23.4% in Høje-Taastrup. The reports also point to regional equalisation payments, which redistribute funds between councils but do not remove concerns about the long-term balance.

content.headline: Aarhus University investigates assault on Muslim researcher
content.shortHeadline: Aarhus University researcher was assaulted after threats
content.standfirst: A younger researcher with a Muslim background was attacked on campus after their institute received anonymous threats. Police are investigating whether it was a hate crime; no suspect has been arrested or charged.

image.caption: The reported assault took place at Aarhus University’s Nobelparken campus.

sources.originalTitle: Muslimsk forsker overfaldet på Aarhus Universitet

segments.body: A younger researcher at Aarhus University was physically assaulted on campus in late May, the university’s publication Omnibus reports. The institute had previously received anonymous threats directed at the researcher, according to institute head Marie Vejrup Nielsen.

The researcher, who has a Muslim background, needed an extended period away from work, Nielsen said. She could not say whether the researcher’s background was a motive; that is for police to investigate. East Jutland Police says it is examining whether the assault may have been a hate crime. No one has been arrested or charged.

content.headline: First intact fish fossil found in Faxe Limestone Quarry
content.shortHeadline: Rare intact fish fossil discovered at Faxe quarry
content.standfirst: A fossil collector found a complete fish in a 20-kilogram block of limestone, a first for the quarry. Experts have identified it provisionally as a scorpionfish dating back about 63 million years.

sources.originalTitle: Vild opdagelse i kalkbrud

segments.body: A German fossil collector has found an intact fish fossil at Faxe Limestone Quarry, the first complete fish found there, according to TV 2. The 20-kilogram block was brought to KALK Museum, where museum curator Jesper Milàn said the discovery was a surprise after years of saying a complete fish had not been found at the site.

segments.title: Why it may have survived
segments.body: German experts have assessed the fossil as a scorpionfish. Milàn suggests its poisonous dorsal spines may have made it less likely to be eaten, while the species’ partly buried way of life may have helped it remain intact. The skeleton is due to be assessed by the national Danekræ committee.

content.headline: Swedish experts say fatal Copenhagen assault could have brought manslaughter
content.shortHeadline: Swedish experts say fatal assault could mean longer sentence
content.standfirst: A Danish court gave Nkumba Ludovic Tshiembe one year for a punch that killed Swedish police officer Christian Zedig. Swedish legal experts say the case could have included negligent manslaughter under Swedish law; Danish ministers are considering a change to sentencing rules.

image.caption: Christian Zedig, a Swedish police officer and father of two, died after the assault.

sources.originalTitle: I Sverige kunne "uagtsomt manddrab" have været en del af dommen, siger ekspert

segments.body: Nkumba Ludovic Tshiembe was sentenced to one year in prison in Denmark for simple assault after a punch to Christian Zedig’s neck caused the Swedish police officer’s death. Swedish legal expert Johanna Björkman told TV4 the case could have been treated as assault, or aggravated assault, combined with negligent manslaughter under Swedish law.

segments.title: Debate over sentencing
segments.body: Swedish legal reporter Fredrik Sjöshult also said a Swedish court would likely have considered aggravated assault and gross negligent manslaughter, with a longer sentence. Denmark’s Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen called the Danish sentence unacceptably low and said he would propose tougher penalties in cases of simple assault causing death when the offender has prior convictions.

perspectives.body: The report centres on the contrast with Swedish law and public reaction there, where support campaigns have raised money for Zedig’s widow and two daughters. It also notes that Sweden recently increased penalties for negligent manslaughter.

segments.body: Tshiembe had previous convictions, including for serious violence and attempted murder, according to TV 2. The Danish prosecutor had sought a one-year sentence and said justice had been served, despite describing the death as senseless. The supplied reporting does not include a response from the prosecutor to the Swedish criticism.

content.headline: Denmark cannot locate 78,000 debtors living abroad, agency says
content.shortHeadline: Tax agency lacks addresses for 78,000 debtors abroad
content.standfirst: The Danish Debt Collection Agency cannot locate four in ten people abroad who owe the state money, according to records obtained by TV Syd. The number with an unknown address has risen from 49,000 in 2016.

sources.originalTitle: Tusindvis skylder Danmark penge – men styrelse aner ikke, hvor de bor

segments.body: The Danish Debt Collection Agency has no address for 78,000 of the 200,000 people living abroad who owe the Danish state money, according to information obtained by TV Syd. The number whose location is unknown has risen from 49,000 in 2016.

segments.title: Difficult to pursue debts overseas
segments.body: People leaving Denmark with debt are asked to provide their new address, but the agency cannot compel them to do so. Officials say it is difficult to find people who move again and to obtain help from foreign authorities. The agency has contacted embassies and searched its own records for updated details.

content.headline: Man City players focus on football as clubs question political comments
content.shortHeadline: Man City focus on football amid appeal concerns
content.standfirst: Enzo Maresca says Manchester City's players are concentrating on football after the club's guilty verdict. Separately, some Premier League clubs have voiced concern about comments by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

image.caption: Enzo Maresca replaced Pep Guardiola as Manchester City manager.

sources.originalTitle: Maresca says 'feeling is fantastic' among Man City squad
Clubs fear political interference in Man City appeal

segments.body: Manchester City head coach Enzo Maresca says his squad are focused on football and are not worried by the “noise” around the club, which has launched an appeal after being found guilty of the majority of 115 Premier League charges. The international players returned to training nine days after the verdict was published.

segments.title: Concern over the appeal process
segments.body: Some senior club figures told BBC Sport they were concerned that Burnham's comments about the prospect of the club's owners selling up could amount to political interference. Burnham said the football issues must be considered seriously and the process must be independent. City's appeal will be heard by a separate independent appeal board.

perspectives.body: One senior club source said there was “a degree of concern” about the comments; another believed the scrutiny now surrounding Burnham made interference impossible. The accounts reflect different views among club sources, not a finding that the process has been influenced.

content.headline: Senegal's Afcon title appeal will not be decided immediately
content.shortHeadline: No immediate ruling on Senegal's Afcon title appeal
content.standfirst: The Court of Arbitration for Sport has heard Senegal's challenge to the decision awarding the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations title to Morocco. The court says a verdict will not come on the day of the hearing.

image.caption: Sadio Mané was named best player at the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations after Senegal's win.

sources.originalTitle: Afcon final to play out in court - when will Morocco or Senegal be crowned champions?

segments.body: Senegal is appealing the decision by the Confederation of African Football's appeals board to overturn its 1-0 extra-time win over Morocco in January and award Morocco a 3-0 victory. The match had been disrupted after Senegal's coach led some players and staff off the pitch during stoppage-time protests; play later resumed and Senegal won.

segments.title: What happens next
segments.body: The Court of Arbitration for Sport heard the appeal in private. It warned that a ruling would not be delivered on the day of the hearing. Its code says appeal decisions should be issued within four months, although panels are encouraged to work faster. The outcome could reverse Caf's decision; Caf president Patrice Motsepe has said the organisation will respect it.

content.headline: BBC investigation finds Cambodian workers making official football shirts for a
content.shortHeadline: Cambodian workers making official shirts earn under £1 an hour
content.standfirst: A BBC Sport investigation traced official kits for major clubs to two factories in Cambodia. Workers described low pay, heat and pressure over production targets; the companies and Adidas gave responses.

image.caption: Official shirts for clubs including Celtic, Arsenal and Liverpool were traced to factories in Cambodia.

sources.originalTitle: Inside the £1-an-hour official football shirt factories

segments.body: Workers at two Cambodian factories that make official shirts for clubs including Arsenal, Celtic, Liverpool and Real Madrid told BBC Sport they receive basic monthly salaries of $210-$220 (£158-£166), equivalent to less than £1 an hour. Some said they struggled to cover living costs and described factory temperatures above 35C, verbal abuse over missed targets and safety concerns.

segments.title: Pay and company responses
segments.body: The factories' reported salaries comply with local minimum-wage laws; three payslips showed total monthly earnings of about $300 (£226) once overtime and allowances were included. Trax said its average employee earnings were $305-$342 this year. Adidas said it audits suppliers and works with them on improvements; it also said its standards prohibit harassment. Bowker did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

content.headline: Ella Toone recalled to England squad after late call-up; Lucy Bronze withdraws
content.shortHeadline: Toone recalled to England squad; Bronze withdraws
content.standfirst: Ella Toone joined England in Greece after being left out of the initial squad for the World Cup play-off. Lucy Bronze has since returned to Chelsea to manage a minor injury.

image.caption: Ella Toone has made 69 England appearances since her debut in February 2021.

sources.originalTitle: Toone comes into England squad as Bronze withdraws

segments.body: Manchester United midfielder Ella Toone was called into Sarina Wiegman's squad on the eve of the first leg against Greece, after initially being omitted alongside Chloe Kelly. Wiegman said she was impressed by Toone's response to the disappointment: the midfielder trained in Spain and wanted to do what was needed to earn a recall. Toone has 69 England appearances and 24 goals.

Chelsea defender Lucy Bronze has left the squad to manage a minor injury sustained in a league match against West Ham. The second leg of the play-off is scheduled for Leicester on 13 October; the winner will advance to a further two-leg tie for a place at next year's Women's World Cup.

content.headline: Harry Kane targets 100 England goals after equalling appearance record
content.shortHeadline: Kane targets 100 England goals after reaching 125 caps
content.standfirst: Harry Kane says he could reach 100 goals for England after equalling his country's appearance record of 125. Morgan Rogers and Jude Bellingham praised the striker.

sources.originalTitle: 'Amazing' Kane targets 100 international goals

segments.body: England striker Harry Kane has equalled his country's appearance record, reaching 125 caps, and says 100 international goals could be within reach. Team-mates Morgan Rogers and Jude Bellingham praised him. The gathered report gives no further detail on their comments or Kane's route to the target.

content.headline: Everton's Martin Sherif fined £5,000 over 61 betting-rule breaches
content.shortHeadline: Everton forward Sherif fined £5,000 over betting breaches
content.standfirst: The Football Association fined Everton forward Martin Sherif after he admitted causing, permitting or enabling 61 bets. He said he did not place the bets himself, but that they came from accounts in his name that he funded.

image.caption: Martin Sherif joined Everton's youth set-up in 2019.

sources.originalTitle: Everton's Sherif fined for breaching betting rules

segments.body: Sherif, 20, was fined £5,000 by the FA for breaches over a 15-month period from November 2024 to February 2026. He said he did not place any bets himself, but admitted they came from accounts in his name and which he funded. An independent regulatory commission said he had shown “genuine remorse”.

content.headline: Granit Xhaka accepts suspended fine over forged Covid-19 certificate
content.shortHeadline: Xhaka accepts suspended fine over Covid-19 certificate
content.standfirst: Sunderland captain Granit Xhaka says he has accepted a suspended fine of 150,000 Swiss francs for obtaining a forged Covid-19 certificate in 2022. He says the fine is suspended for two years if he commits no further offences.

image.caption: Granit Xhaka joined Sunderland from Bayer Leverkusen in July 2025.

sources.originalTitle: Suspended fine for Xhaka over Covid-19 certificate

segments.body: Xhaka said he accepted the decision and took responsibility for obtaining a false certificate. He said the 150,000 Swiss franc fine is suspended for two years provided he commits no further offences, and that he has paid the court costs. The Swiss public health office said certificates were not generally required by law, but were needed for access to some activities, venues and travel.

content.headline: Rising ticket and TV costs are making sport harder for UK fans to access
content.shortHeadline: Why attending and watching sport is getting more expensive
content.standfirst: Prices for major events and the number of subscriptions needed to watch sport have increased. BBC Sport examines the costs facing fans and the arguments from organisers, broadcasters and rights experts.

image.caption: The cost of attending and watching sport in the UK is under scrutiny.

sources.originalTitle: Ticket rises and more TV packages - why is price of sport increasing?

segments.title: Tickets to major events
segments.body: The report gives examples of advertised 2027 prices: at least £115 for a day of the Ashes at Edgbaston, £255 for a standard Wimbledon singles-final seat and £289 for general admission on race day at Silverstone. A BBC Sport website poll found 95% of respondents thought 2027 Ashes tickets were too expensive. One fan said he would not attend.

segments.title: Costs and access
segments.body: Organisers point to higher operating costs: the R&A says it costs 25% more to stage The Open than five or six years ago. Meanwhile, watching all Premier League, Champions League and Scottish Premiership matches in the UK can require subscriptions to Sky Sports, TNT Sports, Amazon Prime and Premier Sports, as well as a TV licence for other matches. A rights consultant warned that higher prices and fragmented access could encourage piracy.

content.headline: The Avalanches turn jingles, old tech and memory into a new pop odyssey
content.shortHeadline: The Avalanches build an album around memory and old technology
content.standfirst: On No Bad Memories, the sample-driven Australian trio turn computer sounds, jingles and fragments of pop into a frenetic new record—and made a companion film with Haley Joel Osment.

image.caption: The Avalanches’ Robbie Chater, who says their sampled sounds hold memories and human feeling.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Spend time going down rabbit holes’: how the Avalanches created their wildest album yet

segments.title: A record that skips ahead
segments.body: The Avalanches’ new album, No Bad Memories, draws on the sounds of advertising and outdated technology: jingles, audio logos, computer drones and video-game bleeps. Robbie Chater and Tony Di Blasi say they wanted something brighter and more playful than their previous record, shaping the songs to move on abruptly, as if the listener were skipping through a playlist.

segments.title: A world built from samples
segments.body: The record’s musical palette reaches from children’s science television to Tunisian footwork, with guests including John Glacier, Khadija Al Hanafi, Panda Bear and Haruomi Hosono. The band say clearing samples has become increasingly difficult and costly; after finishing the album, they swore off the process—then immediately started sampling again.

segments.title: The film beside the album
segments.body: A 35-minute companion film, directed by the Avalanches with Jonathan Zawada, stars Haley Joel Osment as an employee of a fictional digital archive. The story follows him as he collects people’s possessions and begins to lose track of which memories are his and which have been shaped by the advertisements he has absorbed.

content.headline: Helen’s new album finds Liz Harris making room for friendship and noise
content.shortHeadline: Helen’s Linda’s Head makes room for Liz Harris to sing out
content.standfirst: Grouper’s Liz Harris returns with her dream-pop trio Helen, whose second album brings her lyrics forward without losing its enveloping sound. The band’s collaborators describe the collective process as restorative.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Helen and Grouper.

sources.originalTitle: Linda’s Head
‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Linda’s Head, the second album by Helen, gives Liz Harris’s voice and lyrics more definition than the trio’s 2015 debut. Pitchfork hears a set of concise phrases and vivid images—stars, storms and horizons—inside music that still swells and engulfs the listener. Its review finds the group’s increased clarity does not diminish shoegaze’s enveloping force.

perspectives.body: In an interview, Harris describes Helen as a welcome contrast to Grouper’s solitary process: playing with friends lets her show a more playful side, and rehearsals helped lift her spirits while she was dealing with medical difficulties.

segments.title: The risk of being heard
segments.body: The album’s brighter moments sit beside its darkness, including songs prompted by a dead shark Harris saw on the coast. Harris also discusses the risks of a sudden online audience: a fraudulent upload of her song “Poison Tree” reportedly earned around six figures before she and her label shut the scam down and recovered what she was owed.

content.headline: Jamie T looks back on his early career—and the cost of touring Europe
content.shortHeadline: Jamie T reflects on 20 years of music and costly touring
content.standfirst: The singer-songwriter’s new album revisits the music and anxieties of his early career. He says the expense of touring with a band means he can no longer make European dates work financially.

image.caption: Jamie T, whose album Ghosts (100 Days of Morning) looks back on his career.

sources.originalTitle: Jamie T: ‘I can’t afford to tour Europe anymore’

segments.body: Jamie T’s sixth album, Ghosts (100 Days of Morning), looks back on the period when he began making music as a teenager. He says he wanted to bring that chapter to a close and move on. The song “Tallahassee” folds references to Paul Heaton, Lily Allen and Liam Howlett into a reflection on the moments that made an artist’s life feel iconic.

segments.title: A career shaped by anxiety
segments.body: Treays describes panic disorder as a constant difficulty during his early touring years. He still experiences anxiety, he says, but not at the same intensity. He also recalls how the pressure of a major hometown show prompted him to write, turning self-doubt into the starting point for “Tallahassee.”

segments.title: The economics of getting on the road
segments.body: The musician says ticket sales are his main source of income, but touring with a band is expensive. He has not toured Europe since Brexit, and says the numbers do not currently add up for a run of dates there. He would like to take the new album beyond the UK, but is frustrated that doing so is not financially viable.

content.headline: Interpol find new colours in their eighth album, This Mirror Weighs a Ton
content.shortHeadline: Interpol reshape their sound on This Mirror Weighs a Ton
content.standfirst: After years in the shadow of their early records, Interpol say new collaborators and a return to writing in New York helped open fresh paths on their eighth album.

image.caption: Interpol’s Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler.

sources.originalTitle: Interpol: ‘People romanticise the Noughties music scene. We weren’t all friends’

segments.body: This Mirror Weighs a Ton keeps Interpol’s angular guitars and tense post-punk, while opening space for piano ballads, woodwind, glockenspiel and, for the first time, acoustic guitar. The band’s Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler call the album a product of new creative choices, including bringing touring bassist Brad Truax into the writing process and working closely with producer Andrew Wyatt.

segments.title: A return to familiar ground
segments.body: Writing and recording in New York for the first time since 2014 brought the band back to places tied to their early history. Banks and Kessler also reflect on the much-romanticised New York indie scene of the early 2000s: they remember sharing clubs with other bands, but say the idea that everyone was close friends was not quite true.

segments.title: Art, technology and sincerity
segments.body: Banks says he is sceptical of using AI to make art for the sake of selling it, while Kessler says listeners remain curious about the person and choices behind a piece of music. The album’s lyrics also engage with contemporary unease, including Banks’s response to graphic footage of war he encountered online.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s final album becomes a closing chapter after Dave Ball’s death
content.shortHeadline: Soft Cell’s Danceteria is a final album after Dave Ball’s death
content.standfirst: Marc Almond says he will not make another Soft Cell record without his longtime bandmate. Their newly released album revisits the duo’s formative New York years and the club culture that shaped them.

image.caption: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond and Dave Ball.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Soft Cell had finished Danceteria when keyboardist Dave Ball died in his sleep in October 2025, two days after he and Marc Almond agreed the record was complete. Almond calls it the duo’s sixth and final album, saying he would not make another Soft Cell record without Ball. He remembers feeling numb when he heard the news.

segments.title: New York remembered
segments.body: The album looks back to the pair’s time in New York in the early 1980s, especially the club Danceteria. Almond describes the city’s underground nightlife as exhilarating and creative, but also lonely and increasingly shadowed by the AIDS crisis. The record balances dance-pop celebrations with songs about isolation, escape and regret.

segments.title: An ending they made together
segments.body: Almond says the pair had grown closer while making the album, and that finishing it together feels like a fitting way to close their shared musical story. Their final concert was at the Rewind Festival in August 2025, two months before Ball died; Almond says Ball was in good spirits about the finished record.

content.headline: Jonny Greenwood’s classical curiosity continues to shape his guitar playing
content.shortHeadline: Jonny Greenwood on Steve Reich, Radiohead and learning to play
content.standfirst: As he prepares to perform Steve Reich’s music with the London Sinfonietta, the Radiohead guitarist reflects on the classical influences, arranging choices and daily practice behind his wide-ranging work.

image.caption: Jonny Greenwood, who is performing Steve Reich’s music with the London Sinfonietta.

sources.originalTitle: Jonny Greenwood: ‘In the early days of Radiohead I was a lazy guitar player’

segments.body: Jonny Greenwood is preparing to perform Steve Reich’s music, including “Electric Counterpoint” and “Radio Rewrite,” with the London Sinfonietta. Reich reworked Radiohead material in the latter piece; Greenwood calls that response from a major composer “insanely complimentary.” He has also traced Reich’s influence in Radiohead songs such as “Let Down” and “Weird Fishes/Arpeggi.”

segments.title: The arranger’s ear
segments.body: Greenwood says his role in Radiohead is often less about finding space for a guitar part than about working out what a song needs. He describes Thom Yorke bringing a song such as “Pyramid Song” to the group and the band’s shared task as avoiding anything that would make it worse. He is also preparing a violin concerto and a string quartet.

segments.title: From reluctant player to daily practice
segments.body: Greenwood says he once felt clumsy and lazy as a guitarist, and distrusted technical fluency. Repetition changed that: he now plays guitar every day and says he has become hooked. His musical education also includes the classical composers and analogue synthesizers he encountered before leaving university to tour with Radiohead.

content.headline: Victoria Monét reaches for a sweeping love record on Frequency of Love
content.shortHeadline: Victoria Monét expands her sound on Frequency of Love
content.standfirst: Monét trades some of the playful confidence of Jaguar II for an expansive, often earnest exploration of romance. Pitchfork praises her range while finding that 22 tracks sometimes blur together.

sources.originalTitle: Frequency of Love

segments.body: Frequency of Love stretches Victoria Monét’s polished retro R&B into ballads, interludes and slow jams. The review hears a singer newly willing to state her feelings plainly, with songs that lean into devotion and vulnerability rather than the mischievous persona of her earlier Jaguar records.

segments.title: Ambition and excess
segments.body: Strings, chimes and shifting musical references give the album a cinematic scale. The review singles out “I Want You” for updating quiet storm, and “Reach Out” for its contemporary groove. But at 22 tracks, the project can feel diffuse: similar muted backdrops make some songs run together, and a few guest appearances do little to sharpen Monét’s own distinctive presence.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s debut gets a revealing, if oversized, anniversary reissue
content.shortHeadline: A vast new set reveals how Elvis Costello found his voice
content.standfirst: A 104-track My Aim Is True edition traces the making of Costello’s 1977 debut through demos, live recordings and alternate versions. Pitchfork finds fresh insight in the scale, despite diminishing returns on its later discs.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The new five-CD My Aim Is True edition puts Costello’s debut in the context of the songs and experiments that came before it. Its demos and early recordings make a case for him as a developing craftsman rather than a sudden, fully formed talent, drawing on American songwriters and pub rock before punk sharpened his public persona.

segments.title: The case for the box
segments.body: The review finds the first two discs especially illuminating: the original album’s sharp, restless songwriting and a collection of earlier material that reveals how it took shape. Later discs, documenting the Attractions and a reunion performance, are more appealing to dedicated fans than essential to the story. The set’s scale is both a pleasure and a reminder of the familiar reissue cycle.

content.headline: Can Ali G still make character comedy work on the big screen?
content.shortHeadline: Ali G’s return tests the future of character comedy
content.standfirst: Sacha Baron Cohen’s new film revives a character built on undercover provocation. Its reception may say as much about the prospects for personality-led cinema as about whether Ali G’s satire still lands.

image.caption: Sacha Baron Cohen as Ali G in Ali G: Who Iz I?

sources.originalTitle: Can Ali G: Who Iz I? save character comedy cinema?

segments.body: Ali G returns in Who Iz I? at a moment when character-led comedy has largely disappeared from cinemas, despite surviving on television through figures such as Alan Partridge and Philomena Cunk. The film’s challenge is twofold: to make its central persona feel relevant again and to show that a comedy built around one performer’s creation can still draw an audience.

segments.title: A changed target
segments.body: The character once satirised the appropriation of Black British culture, but critics have long argued that the joke could also reinforce the caricatures it set out to mock. The article weighs whether Baron Cohen can update Ali G for a more polarised and culturally alert moment, without losing the comic tension that made the character work.

segments.title: A tradition of transformation
segments.body: The piece traces character comedy from Charlie Chaplin and Peter Sellers to Austin Powers and Borat, arguing that disguise and performance can expose the anxieties of a period. It remains uncertain whether Who Iz I? can do that now: the film’s full approach and targets are not yet clear from the material discussed.

content.headline: The Uprising turns the Peasants’ Revolt into a muddled Robin Hood myth
content.shortHeadline: The Uprising’s Peasants’ Revolt becomes a messy Robin Hood tale
content.standfirst: Paul Greengrass brings his handheld urgency to the 1381 revolt, but the film’s invented ploughman and Robin Hood-like coda leave its historical drama unsure of its purpose.

image.caption: Andrew Garfield as the Ploughman in The Uprising.

sources.originalTitle: The Uprising review – Paul Greengrass turns revolutionary rage into a Robin Hood origin myth

segments.body: Paul Greengrass’s The Uprising follows Wat Tyler and John Ball during the 1381 Peasants’ Revolt, alongside an invented ploughman played by Andrew Garfield. The film’s crowded, dirt-caked style gives the rebels’ anger physical force, but its central figure increasingly reads as a Robin Hood precursor rather than a character grounded in the revolt’s history.

segments.title: A coda that undercuts the revolt
segments.body: Cosmo Jarvis and Jamie Bell play Tyler and Ball, while Tom Hollander brings energy to the king’s adviser Sir Robert Hales. The review finds moments to enjoy in the performances, but argues that the ending—Garfield emerging from the forest with his “merry men”—makes the film’s claim about revolutionary legacy feel oddly softened and disappointing.

content.headline: Big Girls Don’t Cry finds tender detail in a teenager’s online double life
content.shortHeadline: Big Girls Don’t Cry is a tender New Zealand coming-of-age film
content.standfirst: Paloma Schneideman’s first feature follows a rural New Zealand teenager in 2006, as online role-playing and real-life friendships complicate her search for identity.

image.caption: Ani Palmer as Sid in Big Girls Don’t Cry.

sources.originalTitle: Big Girls Don’t Cry review – a New Zealand teenager finds herself in tender coming-of-age tale

segments.body: In Big Girls Don’t Cry, 14-year-old Sid spends a summer break drifting between parties, friends and the awkward business of growing up. At times she enters chatrooms and pretends to be someone else; those online games have consequences beyond the screen. The film also follows her gradual recognition of her queerness without making it a lesson or a revelation.

segments.title: A performance built from small moments
segments.body: The review praises Ani Palmer’s restrained, expressive performance and the film’s attentive visual style. Set before smartphones and widespread social media, the story finds enduring weight in ordinary experiences—lounging with friends, trying something for the first time, or watching oneself change—while leaving Sid’s future open.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning puts Facebook on trial—but not beyond Hollywood’s reach
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning puts Facebook on trial, with limits
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s sequel follows whistleblower Frances Haugen and reporter Jeff Horwitz, but its critics disagree over whether the drama has enough force—and whether Hollywood can mount a genuine challenge to tech power.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: The Social Reckoning review – Aaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel with all-new evil puppet Zuckerberg
The Social Reckoning review: Aaron Sorkin's drama puts Facebook on trial, but it won't change anyone's minds ★★☆☆☆
Will the Zuckerberg, Musk and Altman movies make a dent on tech giant evangelism?

segments.body: The Social Reckoning dramatises Frances Haugen’s disclosures about Facebook and the reporting by Jeff Horwitz that followed. The Guardian’s review finds an entertaining, fast-moving thriller, but argues that Mark Zuckerberg—played by Jeremy Strong—is pushed to the margins and that the film avoids naming Trump or confronting how the political landscape has since changed.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s review is more dismissive: it says the film lacks urgency and tension, and that its whistleblower-and-reporter story is too repetitive to change viewers’ minds.

segments.title: Criticism in a compromised industry
segments.body: A separate Guardian analysis places the film alongside projects about Elon Musk and Sam Altman, asking whether studio attention to tech power amounts to a political stance or an opportunistic bet on growing public scepticism. It points to the commercial ties between technology companies and Hollywood as a limit on how freely the industry can criticise its increasingly influential partners.

content.headline: The Lost Children of Tuam tells a painful story without offering easy closure
content.shortHeadline: The Lost Children of Tuam refuses an easy ending
content.standfirst: Monica Dolan plays historian Catherine Corless in a restrained drama about the deaths and unrecorded burials of children at an Irish mother-and-baby home.

image.caption: Monica Dolan as Catherine Corless in The Lost Children of Tuam.

sources.originalTitle: The Lost Children of Tuam review – deeply serious retelling of Ireland’s devastating tragedy

segments.body: Catherine Corless’s local-history research uncovered death certificates for nearly 800 children who died at St Mary’s mother-and-baby home in Tuam, County Galway, without burial records. The film follows Corless as she investigates what happened at the institution, which housed unmarried women and children between 1925 and 1961.

segments.title: No comfort in the final frame
segments.body: The review praises Monica Dolan’s portrayal of Corless and the performances of survivors, while valuing the film’s refusal to make the story feel tidier or more cinematic than it is. It ends without a consoling sense of closure, leaving the weight of what happened—and the absence of graves—unresolved.

content.headline: James Dean’s vulnerability still cuts through the legend
content.shortHeadline: The James Dean worth remembering is more than an icon
content.standfirst: A new screen version of East of Eden renews attention to Dean’s performance as Cal. This piece looks past the pin-up image to the nervous, vulnerable actor who became a star before he was ready for fame.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: James Dean’s Cal in Elia Kazan’s East of Eden made him a screen icon, but this account argues that his appeal lies beyond the familiar image of a rebel in a red jacket. The actor brought an exposed, unpredictable quality to the role, especially in the scene where Cal reaches for his father after his birthday gift is rejected.

segments.title: Fame before he was ready
segments.body: The piece recounts Kazan’s decision to work with Dean’s personal history, including his troubled relationship with his father, rather than trying to smooth away his mannerisms. Dean died at 24, after three starring roles, and had described himself as frightened of becoming a film actor. His sudden fame and death helped turn a brief career into a lasting mythology.

content.headline: Sense and Sensibility’s new adaptation makes Austen feel close to the present
content.shortHeadline: Sense and Sensibility finds modern tensions in Austen
content.standfirst: Georgia Oakley’s darker adaptation gives new life to Austen’s sisters and their opposing temperaments. An interview with Fiona Shaw adds insight into the film’s pared-back approach and the career shift that brought her to it.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Sense and Sensibility.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility
Fiona Shaw: ‘They didn’t think women were funny when I was young’

segments.body: The new Sense and Sensibility follows sisters Elinor and Marianne as they face financial insecurity and the difficult balance between feeling and restraint. The review argues that Austen’s conflict still speaks to a generation negotiating privacy, public self-presentation and uncertain futures, even if this adaptation is less consistent than the 1995 film.

perspectives.body: Fiona Shaw, who plays Mrs Jennings, says director Georgia Oakley wanted a more pared-back version of the character. Shaw describes her as foolish in manner but kind in intention, shaped by the close-knit community in which she grew up.

segments.title: More than a romance
segments.body: The review finds the sisters’ contrasting responses to love particularly legible now: Elinor’s restraint can cost her the man she loves, while Marianne’s romantic certainty obscures warning signs. Shaw, who has appeared in major stage and screen roles, also reflects on a late-career surge after being told as a young actor that she was too old for Hollywood.

content.headline: Frasier’s Niles and Daphne romance still feels like a comedy classic
content.shortHeadline: The Frasier stars look back on Niles and Daphne’s long romance
content.standfirst: Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce revisit the seven-season will-they-won’t-they story, from the tango that became a favourite to the live-audience reaction when the pair finally kissed.

image.caption: Daphne and Niles in Frasier.

sources.originalTitle: ‘He was devastatingly sexy’: Frasier’s Jane Leeves and David Hyde Pierce on the love between Daphne and Niles

segments.body: Niles Crane’s crush on Daphne Moon began when he first met her in Frasier’s Seattle apartment. Over seven seasons, the show built that attraction into a running romance, delaying its resolution through friendship, misunderstandings and episodes the actors still remember fondly.

segments.title: Timing the payoff
segments.body: Leeves and Hyde Pierce recall rehearsing the tango in “Moon Dance” and the audience’s reaction when Niles and Daphne finally kissed. They say the writers knew when to end the suspense, bringing the characters together before viewers had tired of waiting and giving the series a carefully planned final season.

segments.title: Friends beyond the screen
segments.body: The actors remain close friends, and each speaks warmly about the other’s work and the show’s ensemble. They also reflect on the pregnancy storyline that hid Leeves’s first pregnancy, a choice she says she wishes had been handled differently.

content.headline: Below turns a sea monster into a very silly Newfoundland nightmare
content.shortHeadline: Below is a daft sea-monster horror with a faint climate warning
content.standfirst: Josh Hartnett leads a supernatural thriller about a fishing town, a strange iceberg and a threat from beneath the water. The Guardian review enjoys the pulpy chaos but finds its climate themes submerged.

image.caption: Josh Hartnett as Calvin Penney in Below.

sources.originalTitle: Below review – a killer snot-berg causes chaos for Josh Hartnett

segments.body: Below sends a mysterious iceberg into the harbour of a struggling Newfoundland community. Soon trawlermen are disappearing and body parts are washing ashore; Josh Hartnett plays Calvin Penney, a fisherman whose family history is tied to the town’s earlier maritime tragedies.

segments.title: Monster movie, muted message
segments.body: The review delights in the series’ sea hags, plaid-clad locals and knowingly ridiculous monster premise. It sees hints of a story about warming oceans and a community under pressure, but says those concerns are overwhelmed by the show’s nostalgia, comic gore and creature-feature thrills.

content.headline: Carrie returns as a more sympathetic teen—and divides its reviewers
content.shortHeadline: Carrie’s new series sparks debate over who gets to be a villain
content.standfirst: Mike Flanagan’s eight-part adaptation updates Stephen King’s horror story for social media, but changes to Carrie and her tormentors have divided critics. The debate reaches beyond fidelity to the book to the show’s idea of villainy.

image.caption: Summer H. Howell as Carrie in Mike Flanagan’s series.

sources.originalTitle: Carrie review – the teenage hell-raiser’s glorious return couldn’t come at a better time
Why a new TV version of horror classic Carrie is already annoying people
The Carrie remake made me furious
Cruel torment, depraved violence, evil turns: where did TV’s real baddies go?

segments.body: Mike Flanagan’s Carrie moves Stephen King’s story of a bullied, telekinetic teenager into the present. Summer H. Howell plays Carrie as curious and open to the world after years of home-schooling; the show also gives her mother Margaret and tormentor Chris more context than earlier versions did.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s review finds the added character detail makes the series richer, and sees its focus on online bullying as a reason the story feels relevant now.

segments.title: A question of fidelity—and agency
segments.body: The BBC reports fans’ objections to Carrie’s casting and characterisation, while also citing a horror scholar who argues that the series codes her outsider status in other ways. The i Paper’s reviewer objects more strongly, arguing that the changes drain Carrie of agency and make her revenge less satisfying.

perspectives.body: The i Paper’s reviewer, who describes King’s novel as a personal touchstone, sees the adaptation as a fundamental loss of Carrie’s anger and independence, not simply a modernising choice.

segments.title: The case for frightening villains
segments.body: A wider argument about recent screen villains places Carrie alongside East of Eden and the drama War. It questions a trend toward giving antagonists sympathetic explanations for their behaviour, asking whether empathy can sometimes soften the force of horror and drama.

content.headline: Bake Off’s audience-choice week brings a welcome pinch of chaos
content.shortHeadline: Bake Off shakes up its cosy formula with audience choice
content.standfirst: The first audience-set challenges handed power to viewers rather than judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood. The result was not outright mayhem, but the show’s new tension and unpredictability pleased this critic.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood judge The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Bake Off is toughening up. Good

segments.body: For the first time, Great British Bake Off viewers chose the week’s challenges. The bakers made cheesecakes with family members, faced individual technical tasks using a basic-ingredient cupboard, and were asked to create wearable bakes. The critic sees the experiment as a welcome disruption to the programme’s familiar cosy formula.

segments.title: A little more edge
segments.body: The challenges produced some mishaps, while the judges’ sharper exchanges brought a different energy to the tent. The review notes that Paul Hollywood did not soften his criticism when a cake collapsed, and that Lawson was willing to disagree with him. It argues the series can keep its warmth while allowing more friction and surprise.

content.headline: Richard Armitage finds a new kind of intensity in crime drama Winter
content.shortHeadline: Richard Armitage on playing forensic pathologist Ethan Winter
content.standfirst: The actor discusses his latest ITV role, his attraction to dark characters and the private life he chooses to keep off screen, alongside the uneasy comic edge of his forensic pathologist.

image.caption: Richard Armitage, who plays forensic pathologist Ethan Winter.

sources.originalTitle: Winter’s Richard Armitage: ‘My pillow humping scene was improvised’
